questions.prompt: What is the Laplace transform of a unit step (the signal \(1\) for \(t \ge 0\))?
questions.explanation: Integrate \(\int_0^\infty e^{-st}\,dt = 1/s\), for \(\mathrm{Re}(s)>0\). \(1/(s+1)\) is the transform of \(e^{-t}\). \(1/s^2\) is the transform of a unit ramp. Multiplying by \(s\) is what a derivative does to a transform, not the transform of a step.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that rises from zero and levels off.

questions.prompt: A signal has transform \(F(s) = \dfrac{8}{s(s+4)}\). Every pole of \(sF(s)\) is in the left half-plane. What is \(\lim_{t \to \infty} f(t)\)?
questions.explanation:
The final-value theorem says the limit is \(\lim_{s \to 0} s F(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} 8/(s+4) = 8/4 = 2\). Partial fractions give \(F = 2/s - 2/(s+4)\), so \(f(t) = 2 - 2e^{-4t}\), which settles at \(2\).
• \(8/s\) at \(s = 0\) is undefined. The factor of \(s\) in the theorem cancels the pole at the origin first.
• \(8\) forgets to evaluate the remaining factor at \(s = 0\).
• \(4\) is the pole, not the final value.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that rises quickly and then flattens.

questions.prompt: A signal \(y(t)\) has transform \(Y(s)\) and initial value \(y(0)\). What is the transform of \(\dot y\)?
questions.explanation: Integration by parts on \(\int_0^\infty \dot y\, e^{-st}\,dt\) produces \(sY(s) - y(0)\). The sign on \(y(0)\) is a minus: the initial value is subtracted, not added. \(Y/s\) is the integral rule. Dropping \(y(0)\) is legitimate only when the signal starts at rest.
questions.figure_alt: A decaying curve that starts above zero.

questions.prompt: The ODE \(\dot y + 3y = 6\) has \(y(0) = 0\). What value does \(y\) settle to?
questions.explanation:
At rest \(\dot y = 0\), so \(3y = 6\) and \(y = 2\). By transforms, \(sY + 3Y = 6/s\), \(Y = 6/(s(s+3))\), and \(\lim sY = 6/3 = 2\). The time solution is \(y = 2(1-e^{-3t})\).
• \(6\) is the input, not the steady output. The steady gain of this ODE is \(1/3\).
• \(3\) is the coefficient of \(y\), not the steady value.
• \(18\) multiplies the input by the coefficient instead of dividing.
questions.figure_alt: A curve rising toward a horizontal asymptote.

questions.prompt: What is the Laplace transform of \(\sin(5t)\)?
questions.explanation: \(\mathcal{L}\{\sin \omega t\} = \omega/(s^2+\omega^2)\) with \(\omega = 5\), so the numerator is \(5\) and the constant term under \(s^2\) is \(25\). The cosine transform puts \(s\) in the numerator instead. \(1/(s+5)\) is a real exponential. Using \(\omega^2\) in the numerator double-counts the \(25\).
questions.figure_alt: A sine wave crossing zero at the origin, rising, then falling.

questions.prompt: The ODE \(\dot y + 2y = 0\) has \(y(0) = 4\). What is \(y\) at \(t = 0.5\ \mathrm{s}\)?
questions.explanation:
The solution is \(y = 4e^{-2t}\). At \(t = 0.5\), the exponent is \(-1\), so \(y = 4/e = 1.47152\). The transform is \(Y = 4/(s+2)\), whose inverse is the same exponential.
• \(4 	imes 0.5 = 2\) multiplies by time instead of exponentiating.
• \(4e^{-0.5} = 2.426\) uses the rate \(1\) instead of \(2\).
• \(4e^{-2} = 0.541\) evaluates at \(t = 1\) rather than at \(t = 0.5\).
questions.figure_alt: A smooth decay from a positive start toward zero.

questions.prompt: Use the initial-value theorem on \(F(s) = \dfrac{3s+1}{s^2+4s+5}\). What is \(f(0+)\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\lim_{s \to \infty} s F(s) = \lim_{s \to \infty} s(3s+1)/(s^2+4s+5) = 3\). The inverse is \(e^{-2t}(3\cos t - 5\sin t)\), which equals \(3\) at \(t = 0\).
• The constant \(1\) in the numerator is not the initial value.
• \(5\), the constant term of the denominator, is not it either.
• \(1/5\) would be a final-value misreading. This transform has no pole at the origin, and the initial-value theorem takes \(s\) to infinity, not to zero.

questions.prompt: \(F(s) = 1/(s-2)\). The algebraic limit \(\lim_{s \to 0} s F(s)\) exists and equals \(0\). What is the final value of \(f(t)\)?
options: The theorem does not apply: \(f(t)\) grows without bound
questions.explanation: \(f(t) = e^{2t}\) grows. The final-value theorem requires every pole of \(sF(s)\) to lie in the open left half-plane. Here \(sF(s) = s/(s-2)\) has a pole at \(+2\), so the algebraic limit \(0\) is not the limit of the signal. The numerator \(1\) and the pole location \(-2\) are not values of \(f\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve that starts near one and bends upward.

questions.explanation:
The transform is \(F(s) = 2/(s+3)\). The integral from \(0\) to \(\infty\) is \(\lim_{s \to 0} F(s) = 2/3 = 0.666667\). Directly, \(\int_0^\infty 2e^{-3t}\,dt = 2/3\).
• \(2\) is the initial value, not the area. A faster decay has the same starting height and a smaller area.
• \(3\) is the decay rate.
• \(6\) multiplies them.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that rises and levels off, the shape of an accumulated pulse.

questions.prompt: A storage element obeys \(0.4\,\dot y + y = 7u\). The input \(u\) is a unit step, and \(y(0) = 0\). What does \(y\) settle to?
questions.explanation:
In steady state the derivative is zero, so \(y = 7\). The transform is \(Y = 7/(s(0.4s+1))\), and \(\lim sY = 7\). The \(0.4\) sets the time constant of a first-order step response. It does not change the final level.
• \(7/0.4 = 17.5\) divides by the time constant.
• \(0.4 	imes 7 = 2.8\) multiplies by it.
• \(1\) is the step height, not the gain.

questions.prompt: A mass-spring-damper at rest obeys \(2\ddot y + 8\dot y + 18 y = u\). The force \(u\) steps to \(9\). Using the final-value theorem on \(Y(s)\), what is the steady displacement, in m?
questions.explanation:
With zero initial conditions, \(Y(s) = 9/(s(2s^2+8s+18))\). Then \(\lim_{s \to 0} sY = 9/18 = 0.5\ \mathrm{m}\). At rest the spring alone holds the load: \(18y = 9\). Mass and damping affect the transient, which is the subject of second-order response, not the resting point.
• \(9/8 = 1.125\) divides by the damping.
• \(9/2 = 4.5\) divides by the mass.
• \(18/9 = 2\) inverts the spring law.

questions.prompt: A controller is \(C(s) = 2 + \dfrac{5}{s}\). At what positive number, in rad/s, does its zero sit?
questions.explanation:
\(C(s) = (2s+5)/s\). The zero is the root of \(2s+5 = 0\), so \(s = -2.5\). The positive frequency asked for is \(2.5\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The pole is at the origin, which is what integral action contributes. A later skill uses this zero to shape a PI loop.
• \(5\) is the integral gain, not the zero.
• \(2\) is the proportional gain.
• \(5/2\) written as a pole instead of a zero still has magnitude \(2.5\); calling it \(0\) confuses the zero with the pole at the origin.
